FACT_ID: sec17-F01 | anchor: A01
Pedestrians account for twenty percent of Hawaii's traffic deaths, the people killed are mostly non-drivers, and nearly half of them are younger than fifteen or older than sixty-five [A01].
Why it matters: the twenty percent share and the young-and-old pattern are the chapter's headline statistics.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F02 | anchor: A01
Almost ninety percent of fatal pedestrian crashes happen in the roadway, more than half of them while crossing, and only slightly more than ten percent happen off the roadway [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F03 | anchor: A01
The roadway is the domain of the motor vehicle, and a pedestrian who enters it has no physical protection, so safety depends entirely on the alertness and actions of both pedestrian and driver [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F04 | anchor: A01
Children are quick and see well but do not understand traffic and underestimate a vehicle's danger and force, while older people are often handicapped by poor vision, slow reaction, inability to move fast and greater vulnerability to injury [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F05 | anchor: A01
As a driver you must slow and be ready to stop whenever you see people walking on or crossing the road or children near it, and the law requires you to sound the horn as necessary to warn any pedestrian on the roadway [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F06 | anchor: A01
You must stop for any blind person in the roadway, identified by a white cane or a guide dog, regardless of the traffic signal or the traffic situation [A01].
Why it matters: white cane or guide dog means stop, no matter what the light shows.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F07 | anchor: A01
The law prohibits driving through a pedestrian safety zone and prohibits passing a vehicle that has stopped to let a pedestrian cross [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F08 | anchor: A01
Be especially watchful for children near schools, parks, playgrounds and residential areas, stop on the signal of any school crossing guard, and the law requires watching for pedestrians when turning at intersections and when entering or leaving driveways [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F09 | anchor: A01
Before you or your passengers get out, look for approaching vehicles, and leave the vehicle on the side away from traffic whenever possible [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F10 | anchor: A01
As a pedestrian cross only at crosswalks because jaywalking is illegal, obey all traffic laws and signals as the law requires, and watch for cars at all times because pavement lines and signals do not guarantee your safety [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F11 | anchor: A01
Never start across the street on a green light that has already been showing for some time; wait for the green on the next cycle [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec17-F12 | anchor: A02
The law prohibits entering the street or a crosswalk when vehicles are approaching close by, because they may not be able to stop, and you should look for turning vehicles before crossing and never run alongside or across a street [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F13 | anchor: A02
Walk on the left side of the street facing oncoming traffic, wear bright clothing when walking on or beside a road, stay off the road when under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and keep your children from playing in the street [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F14 | anchor: A02
Standing or walking on the traveled roadway to solicit anything, or to hold a vehicle or a parking place, is prohibited by law [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F15 | anchor: A02
When a school bus is stopped on a highway with its alternating red lamps flashing, every driver in the bus's lane and in all adjacent lanes must stop before reaching the bus and stay stopped until the bus moves on or the red lamps go off, and breaking this law can cost one thousand dollars [A02].
Why it matters: same lane plus every adjacent lane, until the lights stop flashing, with a one-thousand-dollar fine.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F16 | anchor: A02
Vehicles traveling in the opposite direction on a divided highway need not stop for a school bus, a divided highway being two roadways separated by a strip of land or other space not meant for vehicle travel [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F17 | anchor: A02
Drivers out when school buses make their runs should be alert, because children waiting along the road in the morning mean a bus is in the area and waiting children may dart in front of traffic [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec17-F18 | anchor: A03
Bicycles are legally vehicles with all the rights and responsibilities of other vehicles, yet motorists must be extra alert for them because they are harder to see, may ride unpredictably, and show a wide range of riding ability [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F19 | anchor: A03
Bicyclists must ride as near the right edge of the road as practicable but may move into the lane to prepare a left turn, pass another bicycle or avoid an obstacle at the edge, and they may legally ride along the left edge of a one-way road [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F20 | anchor: A03
Riding against traffic is illegal, but many inexperienced bicyclists do it and this behavior causes about twenty-five percent of all bicycle and car crashes, so drivers should watch for wrong-way riders especially when turning [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F21 | anchor: A03
When passing a bicyclist keep at least three feet between the bicycle and your vehicle until safely past, remember the rider may be faster than you think, and avoid the common crash of passing and then slowing to turn right across the rider's path [A03].
Why it matters: three feet is the passing clearance, and the pass-then-right-turn crash is the named hazard.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F22 | anchor: A03
Stay out of bike lanes, especially when turning right at an intersection, look for and yield to bicyclists when crossing a bike lane, do not pass a bicyclist if you are about to turn right, and train yourself to check for overtaking bicyclists at every right turn [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F23 | anchor: A03
Look before opening your car door, because opening a door unexpectedly so as to endanger moving traffic, including bicyclists, is a traffic violation [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F24 | anchor: A03
Treat bicyclists with aloha, since every bicycle on the road means one fewer car, less pollution and potentially one more open parking space at your destination [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F25 | anchor: A03
Bicyclists must obey all signs, signals and traffic regulations, which is the law and also earns respect for their place on the road, and they should always ride with traffic even for a short distance because motorists are not looking for fast bicycles coming from the wrong direction [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F26 | anchor: A03
When turning right, motorists and bicyclists alike often concentrate so hard on traffic from the left that they forget to check for pedestrians coming from the right [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec17-F27 | anchor: A04
A bicyclist slower than normal traffic rides as close to the right edge as practicable, may use the left edge on a one-way road, and may take the travel lane to turn left, avoid hazards, keep pace with traffic, or when the lane is too narrow to share safely with a motor vehicle [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F28 | anchor: A04
On the roadway bicyclists must ride single file, although they may ride two abreast on a bike lane or path wide enough not to impede traffic, and a bicyclist who breaks a traffic law faces the same penalties as a driver [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F29 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists must follow lane markings, leaving a right-turn-only lane when going straight, must have a headlight and rear reflector at night with a rear light, pedal reflectors and light clothing recommended, and must not carry passengers unless the bicycle is equipped for them [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F30 | anchor: A04
Bicycles may not be ridden on sidewalks in business districts, and elsewhere sidewalk riding is allowed only at ten miles per hour or less while always yielding to pedestrians [A04].
Why it matters: ten miles per hour and yield to pedestrians are the sidewalk conditions outside business districts.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F31 | anchor: A04
Wear a bicycle helmet every ride even where it is not legally required, because serious head injury does not require speed or distance, and be predictable by never swerving in and out of parked cars or traffic [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F32 | anchor: A04
Look behind and make sure it is clear before a left turn or a move into the travel lane, use proper hand signals for turning and stopping, and keep at least three feet from parked cars so a suddenly opened door cannot hit you while watching for cars pulling out [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F33 | anchor: A04
Do not wear headphones when riding, because you need to hear traffic and stay alert to potholes, broken pavement and slippery surfaces, and before each ride confirm working brakes, a tight seat and handlebars, and properly inflated tires in good shape [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F34 | anchor: A04
Be visible in bright clothing and never assume a driver has seen you even after eye contact; get a response from the driver so you are sure [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F35 | anchor: A04
A bicyclist may turn left like a motor vehicle, signaling, moving to the center of the lane when safe and completing the turn, or like a pedestrian by riding to the crosswalk, walking the bicycle across and riding on from there [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec17-F36 | anchor: A04
A bicyclist should not pass vehicles on the right, because drivers may not expect or see a rider there, and when traffic is stopped it is safer and more courteous to take a place in line [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0098]

Misconceptions: on a divided highway only traffic going the same direction as the school bus must stop, but on an undivided road every lane adjacent to the bus must stop; a blind person with a white cane or guide dog is given the right of way regardless of the signal; a pedestrian should not start crossing on a stale green light; you may never pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian; bicyclists may legally leave the right edge to turn left, pass or avoid hazards, and may ride the left edge of a one-way street; sidewalk riding is banned in business districts and limited to ten miles per hour elsewhere.

Mnemonics: Twenty percent of Hawaii's traffic deaths are pedestrians; stop for the cane and the dog; red flashing bus means stop in your lane and every adjacent lane, one thousand dollars if you do not; three feet to pass a bicycle and three feet from parked doors; ten miles per hour on a sidewalk outside business districts.

Glossary: pedestrian safety zone (the marked roadway area reserved for pedestrians that vehicles may not enter); jaywalking (crossing outside a crosswalk, which is illegal); divided highway (two roadways separated by land or space not meant for vehicle travel); bike lane (the marked lane reserved for bicycles that drivers must stay clear of); single file (riding one behind another, required on the roadway).

Dynamic facts: the pedestrian and bicycle crash percentages are statistics stated only as this edition prints them; the duties, the school bus law and the fine amount are stable within the printing but belong to the class of facts the legislature can change.
